records.record_text: The Minister of State stated that the United Kingdom had welcomed the reopening of the border by the Southern Rhodesian authorities. The fact that Zambia had itself decided to close the border was entirely a matter for its own decision.
records.political_signal: UK frames Zambia's border closure as a unilateral decision while welcoming Southern Rhodesia's border reopening.
records.policy_implication: UK distances itself from liability regarding Zambia's alternative transport burden.

records.record_text: The Minister of State recalled that the United Kingdom was trying to persuade the Rhodesian regime to agree to the 1971 Settlement Proposals. Although it had responsibility for Southern Rhodesia, it had had no responsibility internally, for many years, and could not force a settlement.
records.political_signal: UK acknowledges formal legal responsibility but disclaims internal executive enforcement power in Southern Rhodesia.
records.policy_implication: Limits direct UK military or police intervention options in Southern Rhodesia.

records.record_text: With reference to the request of the Special Mission to visit Southern Rhodesia, the Minister stated that such a request could not be implemented since the United Kingdom had no power on the ground.
records.political_signal: UK cannot facilitate access to Southern Rhodesia for UN missions.
records.policy_implication: Mission restricted to visiting neighbouring countries.

records.record_text: The Secretary-General of the Commonwealth pointed out that the Zambian Government had not taken the initiative in the new confrontation... The Zambian Government was taking the position that it could not be expected to rely, for essential imports and exports, on a route that could be opened and shut irresponsibly and without consultation.
records.political_signal: Commonwealth validates Zambia's policy to bypass Southern Rhodesian routes permanently.
records.policy_implication: Strong international political support for alternative transport network.

records.record_text: The Foreign Minister stated that Zambia was a land-locked country bordered by Angola, South Africa, Southern Rhodesia and Mozambique, which were under hostile white minority regimes, placing Zambia in an extremely vulnerable position to violations of her territorial integrity.
records.actor_source: E. H. K. Mudenda (Foreign Minister of Zambia)
records.political_signal: Zambia highlights its geographic exposure as a frontline state against minority regimes.
records.policy_implication: Underscores need for international security and economic guarantees.

records.record_text: The Foreign Minister said that Zambia had made it quite clear that what was happening in Southern Rhodesia was the result of political consciousness on the part of the people of Zimbabwe in their quest for freedom, and freedom-fighters were based inside Southern Rhodesia itself.
records.actor_source: E. H. K. Mudenda (Foreign Minister of Zambia)
records.political_signal: Rejects Smith regime allegations that liberation attacks originate from Zambian territory.
records.policy_implication: Refutes pretext used by Southern Rhodesia for aggressive border actions.

records.record_text: The Minister of Defence and representatives presented detailed accounts of six land mine explosions occurring on Zambian territory since 9 January 1973, causing 7 deaths and over 14 serious injuries, as well as constant military air and water space violations by Southern Rhodesian and South African forces.
records.actor_source: A. G. Zulu (Minister of Defence of Zambia)
records.political_signal: Provides direct factual evidence of hostile external military incursions into Zambia.
records.policy_implication: Supports UNSC condemnation of Southern Rhodesia and South Africa.

records.record_text: The Special Mission inspected sites of land mine explosions at Kazungula and Chirundu/Chiawa/Chilimanga, confirming craters, destroyed civilian and military vehicles, loss of life, and severe injuries to innocent civilians.
records.political_signal: First-hand UN verification of hostile land mine activities inside Zambian territory.
records.policy_implication: Validates Zambian complaint before the UN Security Council.

records.record_text: During the audience with President Kaunda, two convicted prisoners were introduced who confessed in court to being recruited and paid by Southern Rhodesian forces to plant land mines inside Zambia.
records.political_signal: Direct judicial and physical evidence linking Southern Rhodesian security forces to covert sabotage in Zambia.
records.policy_implication: Demonstrates illegal subversion conducted by Southern Rhodesian regime.

records.record_text: President Kaunda stated that the battle Zambia was fighting was not solely a Zambian battle: it was a battle of the human race to put things right, asking the international community to rise to its obligation under the UN Charter.
records.political_signal: Frames Zambia's compliance with UN sanctions as a global duty requiring international burden-sharing.
records.policy_implication: Establishes moral and legal grounds for UN assistance under Article 50.

records.record_text: The Prime Minister of Tanzania declared that Ian Smith had instituted savage forms of collective punishment against entire villages in Zimbabwe and that military co-operation between Portugal, Southern Rhodesia, and South Africa had increased, threatening all of Southern Africa.
records.actor_source: R. M. Kawawa (Prime Minister of Tanzania)
records.political_signal: Tanzania warns of an emerging regional military alliance among white minority regimes.
records.policy_implication: Calls for comprehensive UN strategy against colonial and minority regimes.

records.record_text: In a communication to the Special Mission, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of South Africa stated that no military forces had been sent to Southern Rhodesia, but that South African police units had been stationed there since 1967 to combat terrorist threats and would remain until that threat ceased.
records.actor_source: H. Muller (Foreign Minister of South Africa)
records.political_signal: South Africa defends its ongoing security presence in Southern Rhodesia while denying deploying regular military units.
records.policy_implication: Refusal to withdraw police units defies UNSC demands.

records.record_text: The Special Mission concluded under resolution 326 (1973) that a considerable measure of tension continues to exist in the area, the key to the solution of which lies in the application of majority rule in Southern Rhodesia and strict implementation of mandatory sanctions.
records.political_signal: Reaffirms that regional peace is contingent on democratic transition and effective sanctions in Southern Rhodesia.
records.policy_implication: Recommends sustained Security Council pressure and sanctions enforcement.

records.record_text: The Special Mission assessed under resolution 327 (1973) that Zambia needs to divert 75,000 tons of monthly imports and normal export traffic to alternative overland routes in Zaire, Malawi, and Tanzania, requiring capital costs of 77 million kwacha ($124 million) for transport equipment and infrastructure.
records.political_signal: Quantifies the major financial capital requirements necessary to sustain Zambia's economic independence from Southern Rhodesia.
records.policy_implication: Serves as the technical baseline for UN and international aid mobilization.

records.record_text: The Special Mission concluded that an airlift carrying 15,000 tons monthly will be needed temporarily at a cost of 4 million kwacha ($6.5 million) per month, alongside additional annual transport cost surcharges of 31 million to 39 million kwacha.
records.political_signal: Highlights the immediate recurring operational deficit faced by Zambia due to route diversion.
records.policy_implication: Urgent appeal for emergency operational grants and technical assistance.

mission_title: Report of the Security Council mission to Colombia, 7–11 February 2024

mission_analytics.mission_subtype: Field Assessment and Political Engagement Mission
main_risks: Persistent violence and competition by illegal armed groups for territorial control and illicit economies
High levels of violence against former FARC-EP combatants, social leaders, and human rights defenders
Delays and backlogs in implementing key chapters of the Final Agreement, particularly comprehensive rural reform, the ethnic chapter, and gender provisions
Fragmentation and delays in transitional justice processes and amnesties
main_commitments: Government commitment to accelerate the implementation of the 2016 Final Peace Agreement
Former combatants' firm reaffirmation not to return to arms despite security risks and delays
Government commitment to advance the 'total peace' policy through dialogues with armed groups (ELN, EMC, Segunda Marquetalia)
Pact for the implementation of the ethnic chapter setting a goal of 60 per cent compliance by 2026
main_policy_signals: The 2016 Final Agreement must remain at the core of peacebuilding efforts in Colombia
Dialogues with remaining armed groups under the Total Peace policy serve as a complementary strategy to expand peace
Transitional justice through the Special Jurisdiction for Peace requires independent support and judicial stability to achieve restorative justice
Sustained United Nations Security Council engagement and verification mandate are critical to keeping the peace process on track
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: The Security Council carried out its third mission to Colombia to assess the implementation of the 2016 Final Peace Agreement and the Government's complementary 'total peace' policy. The mission observed significant historic progress, strong commitment from former combatants and state institutions, and novel restorative justice efforts. However, ongoing violence by illegal armed groups against social leaders, former combatants, and vulnerable ethnic communities, combined with implementation backlogs in rural reform and amnesties, poses serious risks. The mission underscored that accelerating full implementation of the Final Agreement and maintaining State presence in rural peripheries are essential for lasting peace.

activities.activity_description: Briefing by Special Representative of the Secretary-General Carlos Ruiz Massieu, Resident Coordinator Mireia Villar Forner, and the United Nations Country Team in Bogotá on national developments and UN support.
High-level meeting with Government entities responsible for peace implementation in Bogotá, chaired by Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Elizabeth Taylor Jay.
High-level meeting with the President of Colombia, Gustavo Petro, in Bogotá.
Joint press encounter in Bogotá with President Gustavo Petro and Security Council mission co-leads.
Meeting with peace signatories, including leaders and members of Congress from the Comunes Party and former FARC-EP representatives in Bogotá.
Visit and meeting with the President, Vice-President, and magistrates of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) at their offices in Bogotá.
Meeting with members of Congress across political parties in Bogotá on legislative peace initiatives and strategy.
Meeting with the High Commissioner for Peace and Heads of Government delegations to peace dialogues with ELN and EMC in Bogotá.
Attended a performance by 'Hijas e hijos de la paz', a choir of children of former FARC-EP members in Bogotá.

Field visit to the Agua Bonita former territorial area for training and reintegration (ETCR) in Caquetá Department, meeting with ex-combatants, local authorities, and touring productive projects and Humanicemos demining.
Meeting with civil society leaders representing academia, churches, victims, human rights, ethnic groups, and the private sector in Bogotá.
Dedicated meeting with women's organizations and platforms in Bogotá regarding the WPS agenda, gender measures, and peace dialogues.
Field visit to Buenaventura, Valle del Cauca Department, meeting with Vice-President Francia Márquez, local authorities, Afro-Colombian and Indigenous civil society, youth, and victims.
Attended a memorial ceremony led by mothers of disappeared persons during the conflict in Buenaventura.
Video statements to the media issued by mission co-leads from Cartagena de Indias.
Security Council briefing held in New York where co-leads presented observations and assessments following the return of the mission.

records.record_text: The Security Council heard a common assessment by the Mission and United Nations partners that Colombia had made historic progress in the context of its peace process, that the Final Agreement should remain at the core of peacebuilding efforts in the country, that its full implementation was key to addressing current challenges, and that additional dialogue initiatives with armed groups under the current Government’s policy of total peace were a complementary strategy for expanding the scope of peace.
records.actor_source: UN Verification Mission in Colombia and UN Country Team
records.political_signal: Reaffirmation that the 2016 Final Agreement remains the foundational framework for peace in Colombia.
records.policy_implication: Dialogues with armed groups under total peace should complement rather than replace the 2016 Agreement.

records.record_text: OHCHR reported having verified the killings of 105 human rights defenders in 2023; OCHA reported 250,000 internally displaced persons over the same period in the context of continuing competition by illegal armed groups for territorial control and illicit economies.
records.political_signal: Highlighting severe human rights threats and displacement driven by illegal armed group activity.
records.policy_implication: Urgent requirement for protective State presence and security enforcement in vulnerable rural areas.

records.record_text: President Gustavo Petro announced his intention of launching a new dialogue process with the armed group Segunda Marquetalia, a dissident faction of the former FARC-EP whose leaders had subscribed to the Final Agreement and later left the process.
records.political_signal: Expansion of the Total Peace strategy to negotiate with major dissident insurgent factions.
records.policy_implication: May require additional UN monitoring or good offices support if dialogues formalize.

records.record_text: President Petro underscored that land issues were at the heart of the conflict; 3 million hectares of land were to be distributed through rural reform and 7 million land titles needed to be registered, but only 13 thousand hectares of land had been distributed thus far.
records.political_signal: Acknowledgment of major lag in fulfilling core rural reform commitments of the 2016 Agreement.
records.policy_implication: Immediate acceleration and resource allocation needed for agrarian land titling and distribution.

records.record_text: Comunes President Rodrigo Londoño expressed severe concerns over the state of Agreement implementation and delays in amnesties for some 7,000 former guerrilla members, but assured that 'no matter what happens, we will not return to arms'.
records.political_signal: Unwavering political commitment of FARC-EP peace signatories to non-violence despite legal and security frustrations.
records.policy_implication: Need for expedited resolution of pending amnesties and enhanced legal security for ex-combatants.

records.record_text: The Special Jurisdiction for Peace reported that about 70 per cent of former FARC-EP members (some 9,000 people) had been granted amnesties for political crimes, and that the tribunal was preparing to issue its first restorative sentences in 2024 across 11 macro cases.
records.political_signal: Transition of transitional justice into the operational restorative sentencing phase.
records.policy_implication: Preparation for UN Verification Mission to verify compliance with restorative sentences as mandated.

records.record_text: Magistrates of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace invited the Council to maintain its support so that the JEP could maintain its judicial independence amidst political and institutional obstacles.
records.actor_source: Magistrates of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace
records.political_signal: Appeal for international political backing to shield transitional justice from domestic political interference.
records.policy_implication: UN Security Council political messaging should actively defend JEP independence.

records.record_text: Government negotiators briefed the Council that the latest round of ELN talks produced a six-month renewal of the bilateral ceasefire and ELN commitments to cease ransom kidnappings and the recruitment of children aged 15 and under.
records.actor_source: Government Chief Negotiator for ELN talks
records.political_signal: Tangible humanitarian progress in peace dialogues with ELN.
records.policy_implication: Ceasefire verification mechanisms must closely monitor compliance with child protection and kidnapping commitments.

records.record_text: Government negotiators for the EMC talks stated that a six-month ceasefire extension through 16 July 2024 was agreed alongside pledges to cease ransom kidnappings and child recruitment under 15, while hoping the Security Council would authorize UN Verification Mission participation in ceasefire monitoring.
records.actor_source: Government Chief Negotiator for EMC talks
records.political_signal: Formal request for UN mandate extension to cover ceasefire verification with EMC.
records.policy_implication: Security Council consideration of mandate expansion for EMC ceasefire verification.

records.record_text: Women's leaders called upon the Council to monitor and encourage the implementation of gender measures in rural reform, political participation, and the ethnic chapter, underscoring the need for accelerated implementation and dedicated funding for women's organizations.
records.political_signal: Demand for substantive inclusion of WPS agenda in peace agreement execution and ongoing total peace negotiations.
records.policy_implication: UN Verification Mission should enhance targeted tracking of 122 gender measures.

records.record_text: During the visit to Agua Bonita ETCR, ex-combatant leaders highlighted achievements in peaceful coexistence and humanitarian demining by Humanicemos, but cited persistent security risks, stigmatization, and lack of rural reform implementation as major obstacles.
records.political_signal: Highlighting grassroots resilience of ex-combatants alongside acute vulnerabilities to violence.
records.policy_implication: Targeted economic support, security guarantees, and land access needed for former ETCRs.

records.record_text: Vice-President Francia Márquez welcomed the Security Council's expansion of the Verification Mission mandate to rural reform and the ethnic chapter, while noting that ethnic chapter implementation was hampered by lack of clear indicators and benchmarks which should be reformulated.
records.political_signal: State commitment to ethnic community rights paired with operational critique of monitoring frameworks.
records.policy_implication: Reformulation of ethnic chapter implementation metrics and indicators.

records.record_text: Youth and victims' leaders in Buenaventura stressed that young people were lured into gang violence due to poverty, hunger, and absence of education and job opportunities, appealing for humanitarian agreements and protection against forced disappearances.
records.actor_source: Youth and Victims' Leaders in Buenaventura
records.political_signal: Emphasis on root socio-economic drivers of youth recruitment into violent urban gangs.
records.policy_implication: Socio-economic investments for youth must accompany urban gang truce efforts.

mission_title: Report of the Security Council mission to the Republic of Colombia, 11–14 July 2019

main_risks: Killings, threats, and security risks targeting social and community leaders, human rights defenders, and former FARC-EP combatants
Security vacuum and persistent violence in former conflict areas driven by illegal armed groups, drug trafficking, and illegal mining
Threat of government budget cuts impacting transitional justice institutions
Political polarization surrounding the Final Agreement and ongoing legislative/legal attempts to alter its framework
main_commitments: Joint Government and FARC request to renew the UN Verification Mission mandate for one year starting 26 September 2019
Government commitment to maintain stipends, services, and security for former combatants during ETCR transition
Government commitment to honour voluntary coca crop substitution agreements with participating rural families
FARC political party commitment to irreversible participation in the peace process and compliance with transitional justice mechanisms
main_policy_signals: Unanimous Security Council support for the full and integrated implementation of the 2016 Final Peace Agreement
Necessity of extending comprehensive civilian State presence and development into former conflict areas rather than relying solely on military approaches
Strong international backing for the autonomy, independence, and adequate funding of transitional justice institutions
Call for reducing political polarization and accelerating gender-responsive and ethnic-focused peace provisions
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: The Security Council mission to Colombia (11–14 July 2019) expressed unanimous support for the 2016 Final Peace Agreement and received a joint request from the Government and FARC to extend the UN Verification Mission's mandate. The mission evaluated progress in ex-combatant reintegration, FARC political participation, and transitional justice operations, while identifying severe risks from ongoing killings of social leaders and former combatants, security vacuums in former conflict zones, drug trafficking, and political polarization. Stakeholders across government, parliamentary parties, civil society, and local indigenous communities highlighted the imperative of integrated implementation, comprehensive State presence, and robust funding for peace institutions.

activities.activity_description: Breakfast meeting with President Iván Duque Márquez at the Foreign Ministry in Bogotá.
Joint press stakeout by President Iván Duque and Council co-leaders in Bogotá.
Technical meeting with senior government officials involved in peace implementation and stabilization, led by Presidential Adviser Emilio Archila.
Meeting with representatives of political parties from the Peace Commissions of the Senate and House of Representatives.
Lunch meeting with the United Nations Country Team in Bogotá.
Meeting with FARC political party leadership, including President Rodrigo Londoño and congressional representatives.
Meeting with civil society representatives from peace platforms, human rights, Church, women, ethnic groups, youth, and think tanks.
Meeting with leaders of the Comprehensive System of Truth, Justice, Reparation and Non-Repetition (SJP, Truth Commission, Search Unit).
Meeting in Caldono, Cauca Department, with community leaders, social organizations, and ethnic/women representatives.

activities.activity_type: Visit to Community or Project Site
activities.activity_description: Visit to the Santa Rosa territorial area for training and reintegration (ETCR) in Caldono, Cauca, including dialogue with residents and inspection of productive projects.

actors_met.actor_name: Iván Duque Márquez, President of the Republic of Colombia
Senior Government Officials (Foreign Minister Trujillo, Presidential Advisers Archila, Barbosa, Guarín, ARN Director Stapper)

Peace Commissions of Congress (Senate and House Representatives from Centro Democrático, Alianza Verde, Cambio Radical, Partido Liberal, Partido Social de la Unidad Nacional, Polo Democrático, FARC, Lista Decencia, Colombia Justa Libres)
FARC Political Party Leadership (Rodrigo Londoño, Pastor Alape, Pablo Catatumbo, Victoria Sandino, Carlos Antonio Lozada, Jairo Estrada, Rodrigo Granda, Sandra Ramírez)
Civil Society Organizations (Peacebuilding, Human Rights, Catholic Church, Women's, Ethnic, Youth, Think Tanks)
Leaders of Transitional Justice Institutions (Patricia Linares - SJP; Father Francisco De Roux - Truth Commission; Luz Marina Monzón - Search Unit)
United Nations Country Team in Colombia
Community and Indigenous Leaders of Cauca Department (including San Lorenzo Local Indigenous Council Governor Alfonso Díaz)
Residents and former FARC combatants at Santa Rosa ETCR

records.record_text: President Duque stressed that those who had taken part in the 'no' campaign in the 2016 plebiscite were not opposed to peace, but saw the need for changes, promising he would work for a successful peace and not destroy or disrupt the essence of the Final Agreement.
records.political_signal: Reassurance of government commitment to the peace process.
records.policy_implication: Affirms continuity of peace implementation under the current administration.

records.record_text: President Duque cited examples of progress including 24 approved productive projects employing 1,300 ex-combatants, completion of all 16 development programmes with a territorial focus (PDETs), and updating of the land register.
records.political_signal: Demonstrating tangible government results in economic reintegration and rural planning.
records.policy_implication: Validates ongoing government funding and structural projects for ex-combatants.

records.record_text: President Duque recalled his reasons for objecting to several provisions in the Law on the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, but pledged to support and work closely with the transitional justice system after signing it into law.
records.political_signal: Respect for constitutional institutions despite political objections.
records.policy_implication: Ensures institutional backing for SJP functioning.

records.record_text: President Duque expressed concern over the killing of community leaders, human rights defenders and former FARC-EP members in rural areas, noting the challenge was concentrated in 50 municipalities heavily influenced by drug trafficking and illegal mining.
records.political_signal: Acknowledgement of severe security threats facing vulnerable leaders.
records.policy_implication: Targeted security and law enforcement interventions required in high-risk municipalities.

records.record_text: President Duque presented a letter requesting, on behalf of the Government and FARC, the renewal of the United Nations Verification Mission mandate for another year starting on 26 September 2019.
records.political_signal: Joint political agreement between Government and FARC on UN oversight continuation.
records.policy_implication: Triggers Security Council resolution drafting to extend UN Verification Mission.

records.record_text: President Duque welcomed greater international focus on ensuring FARC compliance with obligations under the Final Agreement, including asset reporting, knowledge of drug trafficking routes, and cooperation with the Special Jurisdiction for Peace.
records.political_signal: Call for balanced international scrutiny on former insurgents.
records.policy_implication: Pressure on FARC party to fulfill asset and truth disclosure commitments.

records.record_text: Security Council delegation emphasized unanimous support for the implementation of the Final Agreement, expressed hope that political polarization could be reduced, and stressed concerns about killings of social leaders and former FARC-EP members.
records.political_signal: Unwavering Security Council commitment to Colombian peace process and leader safety.
records.policy_implication: Reinforces international political pressure for full agreement adherence and security protection.

records.record_text: Security Council members voiced support for voluntary crop substitution coupled with alternative development as key to combating illicit drugs, and stressed the importance of the Final Agreement as an integrated package.
records.political_signal: Preference for voluntary substitution over forced eradication/fumigation.
records.policy_implication: Encourages rural development investment over punitive anti-narcotics measures.

records.record_text: Presidential Adviser Archila noted that the National Comprehensive Programme for the Substitution of Illicit Crops (PNIS) had been established without requisite financial resources, but affirmed the Government would honour commitments to families voluntarily eradicating coca.
records.political_signal: Acknowledgment of fiscal constraints alongside pledge to honour state obligations.
records.policy_implication: Requires budget reallocation to meet voluntary crop substitution payouts.

records.record_text: Opposition and independent legislators acknowledged progress in disarmament and FARC political participation, but stated that implementation had been selective, rural reform chapters were neglected, and State security presence in former conflict zones had failed.
records.political_signal: Critique of executive branch's selective peace implementation.
records.policy_implication: Legislative pressure for broader rural reform and non-military State expansion.

records.record_text: Governing party legislators (Centro Democrático) argued that 'no' plebiscite voters' views were still ignored, criticized transitional justice as favoring perpetrators over victims, and blamed the peace agreement for coca expansion and FARC dissident growth.
records.political_signal: Continued ruling party resistance to specific peace agreement provisions.
records.policy_implication: Risk of further legislative attempts to reform transitional justice and drug policies.

records.record_text: FARC party leaders expressed concern that government political will was limited, citing a contrast between international discourse and domestic actions in Congress aimed at undermining the Final Agreement, as well as approved reintegration projects benefiting only 1,655 of 13,415 ex-combatants.
records.political_signal: FARC dissatisfaction with speed and scope of socio-economic reintegration.
records.policy_implication: Urgent need to accelerate productive project approvals and funding disbursement.

records.record_text: FARC party leaders explicitly distanced themselves from former leaders like Jesús Santrich who left the peace process, reiterating that FARC leadership remains committed to peaceful institutional struggle and compliance with transitional justice obligations.
records.political_signal: Rejection of insurgency re-armament and affirmation of political pathway.
records.policy_implication: Isolates re-armed dissident factions from the legitimate FARC political party.

records.record_text: Civil society representatives reported that non-militarized State extension was essential, criticizing inadequate funding for peace, underutilization of the National Commission on Security Guarantees, and severe killings of social leaders disproportionately affecting ethnic communities.
records.political_signal: Civil society demand for integrated security protection and implementation of ethnic provisions.
records.policy_implication: Operationalization of National Commission on Security Guarantees and ethnic self-protection schemes.

records.record_text: President of Special Jurisdiction for Peace Patricia Linares reported that over 11,000 FARC members, 2,000 public security force members, and 53 civilians voluntarily submitted to SJP jurisdiction, with 7 major cases opened involving 830,000 victims.
records.political_signal: Demonstrating institutional efficacy and judicial outreach of SJP.
records.policy_implication: Sustained political and material backing needed as proceedings advance to judicial decisions.

records.record_text: Leaders of the three transitional justice institutions expressed shared concern that announced government budget cuts could severely hamper their operations during their transitory mandates.
records.political_signal: Warning against fiscal strangulation of transitional justice bodies.
records.policy_implication: Exemption of SJP, Truth Commission, and Search Unit from national budgetary austerity measures.

records.record_text: Community and indigenous leaders in Caldono, Cauca attributed ongoing violence to competing illegal armed groups (ELN, FARC dissidents, paramilitaries), drug trafficking, and resistance to ethnic territory/resource defence, urging full rural reform implementation and ELN dialogue.
records.political_signal: Local demand for protection, rural development, and comprehensive peace dialogues.
records.policy_implication: Strengthening Indigenous Guard self-protection, PDET delivery, and conflict resolution mechanisms in Cauca.

mission_title: Report of the Security Council mission to Côte d’Ivoire and Guinea-Bissau

main_risks: Political tensions and shifts in party alliances ahead of the 2020 presidential elections in Côte d'Ivoire.
Root causes of conflict in Liberia remaining unaddressed, compounded by security vulnerabilities and economic fragilities post-UNMIL exit.
Voter registration anomalies, technical discrepancies, and student/teacher strikes creating unrest ahead of Guinea-Bissau's legislative elections.
Rampant corruption, constitutional ambiguity, fragile state institutions, and organized drug trafficking in Guinea-Bissau.
main_commitments: Holding free, fair, and transparent legislative elections in Guinea-Bissau on 10 March 2019 and presidential elections later in 2019.
Implementation of the Conakry Agreement, Stability Pact, and Code of Conduct by Bissau-Guinean political stakeholders.
Support from international partners and UNCTs for residual peacebuilding challenges following peacekeeping mission drawdowns in Côte d'Ivoire and Liberia.
main_policy_signals: Strong Security Council reaffirmation of sovereignty, territorial integrity, and peaceful democratic transition in Côte d'Ivoire.
Call for inclusive political dialogue and constitutional reform in Guinea-Bissau to end recurring executive-legislative deadlocks.
Emphasis on systematic transition planning, capacity mapping of UN country teams, and sustained voluntary/peacebuilding funding when ending UN peacekeeping operations.
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: The Security Council mission to West Africa evaluated post-peacekeeping transition processes in Côte d'Ivoire and Liberia while engaging directly in Guinea-Bissau to support the legislative elections planned for 10 March 2019. In Côte d'Ivoire, the Council observed significant economic growth and successful DDR implementation, while highlighting the need for inclusive dialogue, constitutional alignment, and residual peacebuilding post-UNOCI. In Guinea-Bissau, the mission engaged across the executive, legislative, judicial, electoral, political party, and civil society spectrum to advocate for timely, credible elections, full adherence to the Conakry Agreement, political stability, and capacity building against drug trafficking.

activities.activity_description: Meeting with the Vice-President and the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Côte d'Ivoire in Abidjan.
Round-table discussion on the transition from peacekeeping to peace consolidation in Côte d'Ivoire and Liberia, attended by respective Resident Coordinators.
Meeting with the Prime Minister and key Cabinet members of Guinea-Bissau in Bissau.
Working dinner with representatives of the diplomatic community and the Group of Five in Bissau.
Briefing by the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Guinea-Bissau to the Security Council on UNIOGBIS premises.
Breakfast meeting with representatives of the Group of Five international organizations in Bissau.
Meeting with the Speaker of the National Assembly and heads of parliamentary political parties in Guinea-Bissau.
Meeting with the President of the National Electoral Commission (CNE) of Guinea-Bissau.
Meeting with the Vice-President of the Supreme Court of Justice of Guinea-Bissau.
Meeting with representatives of political parties not represented in the National Assembly of Guinea-Bissau.
Meeting with civil society organizations and the organizing commission of the national conference in Guinea-Bissau.
Working lunch with the United Nations country team and international partners in Guinea-Bissau.
Meeting with the President of Guinea-Bissau, José Mário Vaz, at the Presidential Palace.
Press briefing by the co-leads of the Security Council mission to summarize visit outcomes.

records.record_text: Vice-President Duncan expressed appreciation for the work of the United Nations, in particular UNOCI, for peace and stability in Côte d'Ivoire and suggested that Côte d'Ivoire be used as a model for countries making the transition from peacekeeping to peacebuilding.
records.political_signal: Promote Ivorian transition model as a standard for UN peace operations drawdown.
records.policy_implication: Demonstrates successful transition from UN peace enforcement to national peace consolidation.

records.record_text: Vice-President Duncan stated that the leadership of President Ouattara, national ownership of DDR and SSR, national reconciliation efforts, effective partnership with UNOCI, and close collaboration with neighbouring countries were key factors that contributed to successful transition.
records.political_signal: Highlight strong national ownership as indispensable for post-conflict recovery.
records.policy_implication: National funding and political leadership enable sustainable DDR/SSR transitions.

records.record_text: The Vice-President informed the mission that 93 per cent of former combatants had been reintegrated, while the Government financed 72 per cent of the disarmament, demobilization and reintegration programme over a three-year period.
records.political_signal: Demonstrate high level of state co-financing and commitment to post-conflict stabilization.
records.policy_implication: DDR programs succeed when heavily backed by national fiscal budgets.

records.record_text: Permanent Representative Anatolio Ndong Mba stressed the need for Côte d'Ivoire to ensure a credible electoral process in 2020 for the consolidation of peace and stability in the country.
records.political_signal: UNSC signal that 2020 presidential elections are a major benchmark for consolidating democratic gains.
records.policy_implication: Electoral credibility is essential to prevent conflict recurrence in post-peacekeeping settings.

records.record_text: The resident coordinator for Côte d'Ivoire identified land conflicts and issues related to the management of natural resources as remaining root causes of conflict in Côte d'Ivoire.
records.political_signal: Warn against unresolved structural risk factors following UN mission departure.
records.policy_implication: Land tenure reform and resource governance must be integrated into peacebuilding strategies.

records.record_text: The resident coordinator for Liberia noted that Liberia had not yet fully addressed the root causes of conflict, including issues of accountability and reconciliation, and called upon the Security Council to look at Liberia through 'a lens of prevention and not of celebration'.
records.political_signal: Premature celebration of mission exits risks ignoring structural post-peacekeeping fragilities.
records.policy_implication: UNSC mandates should maintain structured residual peacebuilding and human rights monitoring post-drawdown.

records.record_text: Security Council members co-lead Ndong Mba expressed the hope that the Government of Guinea-Bissau would continue its efforts to promote unity and engage in constructive dialogue for the full implementation of the Conakry Agreement.
records.political_signal: Conakry Agreement remains the key benchmark for political stabilization in Guinea-Bissau.
records.policy_implication: Consensus framework required to prevent constitutional deadlocks.

records.record_text: Prime Minister Aristides Gomes noted that on 14 February competing political parties had signed the Stability Pact, obliging signatories to accept election results and implement institutional reforms regardless of outcome.
records.political_signal: Pact signing serves as an essential guarantee of post-electoral stability.
records.policy_implication: Pre-election political agreements reduce post-election contestation risks.

records.record_text: Prime Minister Gomes acknowledged technical problems with voter registration, explaining that ECOWAS experts were assisting with the audit and cleaning of electoral lists to resolve discrepancies.
records.political_signal: Technical transparency backed by regional bodies is required to protect election credibility.
records.policy_implication: Technical voter list audits mitigate election boycott risks.

records.record_text: Prime Minister Gomes highlighted weak state institution capacity to counteract infiltration and manipulation of social unrest and student protests aimed at disrupting elections.
records.political_signal: Spoilers take advantage of social grievances to derail electoral timelines.
records.policy_implication: Election security arrangements must account for public sector strikes and student unrest.

records.record_text: Prime Minister Gomes noted problems of infiltration within State institutions, making Government efforts to combat drug trafficking and organized crime a challenging task, and called for international assistance.
records.political_signal: Transnational organized crime poses an existential threat to state authority in Guinea-Bissau.
records.policy_implication: Targeted international security support required for island and maritime domain surveillance.

records.record_text: A diplomatic community member highlighted that executive-legislative crisis in Guinea-Bissau stemmed from political interpretation of the Constitution, emphasizing the need for a constitutional referendum.
records.political_signal: Constitutional reform is compulsory to clarify executive powers.
records.policy_implication: Constitutional clarity essential to prevent repeating political deadlocks.

records.record_text: Deputy SRSG noted that in anticipation of UNIOGBIS drawdown by end of 2020, full-scale transition planning would be launched in close collaboration with national authorities and international partners.
records.political_signal: Phased UN mission transition tied to post-electoral stability benchmarks.
records.policy_implication: Joint UNCT-Government transition planning ensures continuity of institutional reform.

records.record_text: The Group of Five noted that legislative elections alone would not resolve the political crisis in Guinea-Bissau without undertaking necessary institutional and constitutional reforms.
records.political_signal: Elections are a necessary step but insufficient on their own to address governance failures.
records.policy_implication: Post-election support must focus heavily on deep structural reforms.

records.record_text: Party for Social Renewal representative Jorge Malu requested an explanation regarding voter registration discrepancies of 200,000 voters compared to 2014, while reaffirming readiness to compete under amended Stability Pact terms.
records.political_signal: Opposition willingness to participate contingent on voter list audit transparency.
records.policy_implication: Audit publication critical to prevent post-election challenge.

records.record_text: CNE President José Pedro Sambú confirmed civic education and polling station staff training were underway, and sensitive election materials would arrive on schedule from Portugal.
records.political_signal: Technical preparations for 10 March elections remain on track.
records.policy_implication: Operational readiness helps secure timely polling.

records.record_text: Vice-President of the Supreme Court Rui Nene indicated that political parties faced difficulties meeting the 36 per cent gender quota due to limited female political participation, but affirmed the Court would strictly enforce parity in future elections.
records.political_signal: Judicial enforcement of legal gender quotas will be mandatory moving forward.
records.policy_implication: Structural capacity building needed to increase women's political candidacy.

records.record_text: Civil society representatives urged the UN not to abandon Guinea-Bissau and appealed for international support to strengthen maritime border controls, combat corruption, and review UN sanctions against 10 military officers post-elections.
records.political_signal: Civil society demands long-term international engagement and selective sanctions review upon democratic progress.
records.policy_implication: Sanctions regime modifications should be benchmarked against security sector compliance.

records.record_text: World Bank representative reported a drop in Guinea-Bissau's economic growth to 3.8 per cent in 2018 due to lower cashew production and falling global prices, emphasizing fiscal frailty and ongoing reforms in public finance management.
records.political_signal: Macroeconomic vulnerabilities compound political instability.
records.policy_implication: Economic diversification and public finance management reforms are vital to state resilience.

records.record_text: President José Mário Vaz stated that all conditions were in place for holding legislative elections on 10 March 2019 and highlighted that the military had remained in barracks due to respect for the chain of command.
records.political_signal: Executive assurance of election timeline and military neutrality.
records.policy_implication: Military non-interference is critical for democratic election credibility.

records.record_text: President Vaz appealed to the Security Council for the lifting of UN sanctions against members of the Guinea-Bissauan military, citing their good behavior and the need to compensate former freedom fighters to facilitate their retirement.
records.political_signal: Head of State advocacy for military sanctions relief as an incentive for reform.
records.policy_implication: Sanctions relief requests require verified military reform and security sector transformation.

records.record_text: The Security Council mission urged Bissau-Guinean political actors to meet obligations under the Stability Pact and Code of Conduct, rectify voter registration irregularities, and proceed with constitutional reform to establish clear separation of executive, legislative, and judicial powers.
records.political_signal: UNSC clear mandate for post-election constitutional rebalancing to prevent systemic governance crises.
records.policy_implication: Constitutional reform must define precise executive powers post-elections.

mission_title: Report of the Security Council Mission to Haiti, 13-16 February 2012

main_risks: Executive-legislative dysfunction and political stagnation hindering elections and state budget endorsement
Slow development, vetting, and recruitment pace of the Haitian National Police leaving internal security capacity fragile
Reports of armed former military personnel occupying former training camps
Widespread severe poverty, massive remaining IDP populations, and vulnerability to seasonal cholera outbreaks
Public frustration and anger over MINUSTAH's alleged role in cholera introduction and sexual exploitation and abuse cases
main_commitments: Reaffirming Security Council commitment to assist Haiti in peace consolidation, democracy, stability, and sustainable development
Implementation of the HNP development plan 2012-2016 jointly drafted by Haitian authorities and MINUSTAH
Government housing pilot programmes (16/6 programme) and proposed social safety net initiatives
Orderly drawdown and reconfiguration of MINUSTAH under resolution 2012 (2011) aligned with HNP capacity building
main_policy_signals: Urging constructive political dialogue between the executive and legislative branches to overcome stalemate and advance key legislation
Stressing that HNP reform and capacity building must be completed to allow national authorities to assume full security responsibility
Emphasizing that any re-establishment of armed forces must undergo a transparent process with civilian oversight and democratic accountability
Enforcing strict adherence to the UN zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse and investigating misconduct allegations
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: The Security Council mission to Haiti (13–16 February 2012) assessed progress in post-earthquake recovery and the consolidation of peace and democracy following the 2011 political transition. The Council observed that while overall security remained stable, deep political executive-legislative dysfunction, delays in holding local/senatorial elections, severe rule of law deficits, and slow HNP recruitment posed persistent challenges. The mission reaffirmed strong support for MINUSTAH while emphasizing the necessity of HNP capacity-building, legal and judicial reform, zero tolerance for personnel misconduct, and political compromise among national leaders.
